text: Every Azure resource has to live somewhere, and Azure organizes its physical datacenters into regions - a choice that affects latency, compliance, and even which services you're able to use at all. Picking a region isn't a throwaway decision made once and forgotten; it shapes performance and legal requirements for as long as that resource exists.

az account list-locations lists every region available to your subscription, along with its display name and the internal name you'll actually type into every CLI command and template - East US shows up as eastus everywhere, lowercase, no space, no exceptions. Getting that internal name wrong is one of the more common typo-driven deployment failures.

A region is a set of Microsoft datacenters inside a defined latency perimeter, connected by a dedicated low-latency network - not every service is available in every region, and not every region is open to every subscription type. Most regions are also paired with another region in the same geography; Microsoft deliberately sequences platform updates across the pair rather than rolling them out to both at once, and prioritizes one region for recovery if the other suffers an extended outage, which matters directly when you're planning disaster recovery.

Naming at scale needs a consistent pattern, not whatever name felt convenient in the moment. az group create --name rg-prod-eastus-web01 and az vm create --name vm-prod-eastus-web01 both follow Microsoft's own recommended convention from its Cloud Adoption Framework: resource type prefix, environment, region, and an instance number, all lowercase and hyphen-separated where the resource type allows it.

Break rg-prod-eastus-web01 down and every single piece tells you something specific: rg says it's a resource group, prod says production rather than test or dev, eastus says exactly which region, and web01 says it's the first web-tier instance. Months from now, anyone - including you - can read that name alone and know exactly what it is, without ever opening the Portal to check.

With regions and naming in place, the last governance piece is keeping costs and compliance under control once hundreds of named resources start piling up across those regions - tags, Azure Policy, and basic cost management, coming up next.
